Daphne Brand Book
DaphneThe brand book ↓

Daphne was a river nymph who wanted to belong to no one.

When a god chased her, she begged to be changed. Her arms became branches. Her hair became leaves.

She became the first laurel tree. Her heart, the story goes, still beat under the bark.

The god wore her leaves as a crown. Since then, laurels have gone to the poets, athletes and artists who were chosen.

Every laurel since is hers. She still belongs to no one, so now she’s free to every filmmaker who’s earned one.

Make festival laurels for your film. It’s free.

The idea

A laurel is two leaves around a name.

Strip away the gold and the ceremony, and that’s what a festival laurel does: it holds a film’s name between two branches and says someone chose it. So our logo holds Daphne’s name inside the leaves she became.

The leaves are brackets, so they can hold anything worth honoring: your film, Official Selection, free. The logo shows the whole job in one shape.

The logo

Her name, held in two bay leaves.

The name is PD Head at 400, light enough to feel classical. Each leaf is a bay leaf on a curved spine, slightly lopsided, with a wavy margin, a hairline midrib and a stalk that bends in under the name.

  • Clear space: one leaf’s width on every side, about a fifth of the logo’s height.
  • Smallest: 96 px wide on screen, 20 mm in print. Smaller than that, the leaves read as plain parentheses, so use the symbol.
  • The gaps are optical: 85 units to the D’s flat side, 66 to the e’s round one.

Don’t

The symbol

(D), for anywhere square.

A heavier D between fuller leaves whose stalks nearly meet under the letter, like a wreath’s crossed stems. Avatars, app icons, the browser tab.

Color

A grove at night, one flower, and no gold.

Festival laurels are gold or silver, so we never are. Green is the living tree; gold is the honor someone earned. When a laurel appears in our frames, it’s the only metal there.

The leaf brackets

Hold one thing.

The logo’s leaves work on their own beside display type. One bracketed phrase a frame, around the thing being honored or given.

Your film got in. Now give it a laurel.
Free for every filmmaker who’s earned one.
  • New leaf on Grove, Bay on Paper. Never Bloom, never gold.
  • Set them at height: 1.24em; vertical-align: -0.30em beside PD Head. Files: bracket/leaf-left.svg, leaf-right.svg.
  • In running text, ordinary parentheses stay ordinary.

Laurels in the brand

Show what she makes.

Every laurel in our material is made with Daphne’s own looks, with words no one could mistake for a real selection. No real festival’s name, logo or artwork, ever.

Motion

Things grow from where they’re attached.

The leaves grow up from their stalks, then the name rises into the room they made, one letter every two frames.

  • Grow, don’t pop. A leaf grows from stalk to tip along its own spine, with a soft growing edge. Nothing scales from its center or slides in from off screen.
  • Leaves first, then words. The leaves grow for 1.05 s; the name starts at 0.5 s.
  • One leaf per frame. A full wreath grows one leaf per frame at 24 fps, so 24 leaves take exactly one second of film.
  • Her heart still beats. In a long hold, the leaves breathe once every 1.2 s, barely. If anything glows Bloom, it’s that beat, and only once.
  • Let one leaf fall. When a piece ends, a single leaf can drift down through the frame. It’s the only exit we use.
  • Easing: growth cubic-bezier(.2,.7,.1,1), words cubic-bezier(.33,0,.15,1). No bounce, no overshoot. Hold the last frame at least a second. Reduced motion shows the last frame.

A 5-second intro or outro, as a starting point

TimeWhat happens
0.0–1.1 sThe leaves grow from their stalks, the right one two frames behind the left
0.5–1.2 sDaphne rises in, a letter every two frames
1.4–2.0 sThe tagline arrives under it: Make festival laurels for your film. It’s free.
3.6 spitch.dog/daphne and Made by pitch.dog
to 5.0 sHold. The leaves breathe once; one leaf may fall.

Words

Plain first. The story is for when there’s room.

Daphne is a person’s name, so it never travels alone: a title, a card, a bio or an end card carries the tagline or the descriptor beside it.

About
Daphne makes festival laurels, the wreaths on a film’s poster that say it was selected for, or won at, a festival. Type the festival, your selection and the year, pick a look, and download it for your poster, trailer and socials as a PNG, SVG, PDF or video. It’s free and works in your browser, with no account and no watermark. Nothing you make leaves your device unless you share it. Made by pitch.dog, and open source.
Why the name
In Greek myth, Daphne turned into the first laurel tree. Every laurel since comes from her.
Credit line
Made with Daphne. Optional, text only, never a logo on someone’s laurel.
Voice
We’re pitch.dog, in the plural. Say what it makes, who it’s for and what it costs, then name the freedoms: no account, no watermark, nothing uploaded. US spelling.

At work

The first places people will meet her.

Files

Everything is drawn by code.

The marks are geometry in brand/tools/mark.mjs, so a change to the logo is a change to the code, never a hand edit to an SVG.
